extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, trade associations, state energy agencies, and other stakeholders participating in DOE rulemaking on consumer water heater standards and commenters to the docket
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative criteria for defining, testing, classifying, and setting energy conservation standards for circulating and other consumer water heaters, and procedural guidance for submitting public comments to the DOE rulemaking docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulating water heater definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Circulating water heater means a water heater that does not have an operational scheme in which the burner, heating element, or compressor initiates and/or terminates heating based on sensing flow; has a water temperature sensor located at the inlet or the outlet of the water heater or in a separate storage tank that is the primary means of initiating and terminating heating; and must be used in combination with a recirculating pump to circulate water and either a separate storage tank or water circulation loop in order to achieve the water flow and temperature conditions recommended in the manufacturer's installation and operation instructions. Paired with a separate storage tank, a circulating water heater constitutes a storage-type water heater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE treats the circulating water heater together with the required separate storage tank or recirculation loop as one system for regulatory classification. Commenters raised concerns that reliance on manufacturers' installation instructions could be too discretionary/enforceable; DOE sought comment on hardware-specific language vs. reliance on documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric circulating water heater definition (thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Electric circulating water heater means a circulating water heater with an input of 12 kW or less; contains more than one gallon of water per 4,000 Btu/h of input (including heat pump-only units with power inputs of no more than 24 A at 250 V).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a numeric input threshold to distinguish electric circulating units; the >1 gallon per 4,000 Btu/h criterion aligns with EPCA's instantaneous/storage volume tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gas-fired circulating water heater definition (thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gas-fired circulating water heater means a circulating water heater with a nominal input of 75,000 Btu/h or less; contains more than one gallon of water per 4,000 Btu/h of input.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nominal input cap (75,000 Btu/h) and volume-per-input threshold are used to classify gas-fired circulating units; DOE also explains how effective storage volume and test-configurations map to condensing vs non-condensing standard stringency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil-fired circulating water heater definition (thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Oil-fired circulating water heater means a circulating water heater with a nominal input of 105,000 Btu/h or less; contains more than one gallon of water per 4,000 Btu/h of input.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric input cap and volume-per-input threshold specify oil-fired unit boundaries for classification under DOE rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test procedure for circulating water heaters (UFHWST pairing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the amended test procedure, circulating water heaters are to be tested with unfired hot water storage tanks (UFHWSTs) with measured volumes between 80 and 120 gallons (see section 4.10 of appendix E); DOE defined effective storage volume as the stored volume of hot water used when testing the circulating water heater (section 6.3.1.1 of appendix E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE chose those UFHWST volumes because standby loss relationships and conversion factors align with storage-water-heater behavior above certain volumes; testing with paired storage reproduces field operation. This test-method choice influences which energy-conservation standard level (e.g., condensing vs non-condensing) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPCA instantaneous-type input and volume limits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPCA defines instantaneous-type water heaters as having no more than one gallon of water per 4,000 Btu/h of input and statutory maximum consumer instantaneous input ratings (e.g., 200,000 Btu/h for gas-fired instantaneous consumer water heaters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE uses these statutory definitions and input caps to show that circulating water heaters, when paired with the required UFHWST volumes, would have effective storage volumes and input relationships that make classification as instantaneous inaccurate under EPCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to establish a separate product class (42 U.S.C. 6295(q) criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE must establish a separate standard for a group of covered products (i.e., a separate product class) based on the type of energy used, or if DOE determines the group has a capacity or other performance-related feature that other products do not have and such feature justifies a different standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deciding whether a performance-related feature justifies a separate standard, DOE must consider the utility of the feature to the consumer and other factors DOE determines appropriate. DOE concluded it had not identified performance-related features for circulating water heaters that would justify a separate product class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer utility as classification criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE distinguishes product classes based on consumer utility: instantaneous water heaters provide a continuous supply up to maximum flow rate; storage water heaters are better for large initial demands rather than continuous draws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE tentatively determined circulating water heaters, when considered with their required stored volume/recirculation components, provide consumer utility akin to storage-type water heaters, supporting classification as storage-type rather than instantaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control-scheme distinction (flow-activated vs thermostatically activated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flow-activated control schemes initiate/terminate heating based on sensing flow and are certified using a maximum GPM delivery capacity; thermostatically activated schemes use water-temperature sensing (inlet/outlet or separate tank) and are certified using a first-hour rating (FHR) delivery capacity metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is central to whether circulating water heaters are considered substitutes for instantaneous water heaters. DOE notes circulating units are thermostatically activated (not flow-activated), supporting storage-type classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective storage volume impacts standard stringency (gas-fired example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For gas-fired circulating water heaters tested with an 80–100 gallon UFHWST, the resulting effective storage volume would generally lead to condensing-level standards; if tested with 100–120 gallon UFHWST, standards correspond to non-condensing efficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE's conversion from test results to standard stringency depends on the UFHWST volume used in testing; commenters argued about implications for market substitution and energy savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE principle on pairing with storage: treat system as single unit
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE treats the circulating water heater plus the separately stored water volume (tank or recirculation loop) as one system operationally similar to storage-type water heaters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: circulating heaters typically have little/no onboard water and rely on separate stored volume for function; thus test and standards should consider effective system behavior rather than heater-only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test/definition parity with split-system heat pump water heaters
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE draws an explicit parallel that split-system heat pump water heaters (heat pump module plus separate storage tank) have long been treated as electric storage water heaters and do not have separate standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precedent supports DOE's tentative decision to classify circulating water heaters as storage-type when paired with storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on substitution claims for gas-fired circulating vs instantaneous heaters
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE found gas-fired instantaneous water heaters typically have flow-activated control schemes and large burners (input rates up to ~200,000 Btu/h) enabling high flow-rate temperature rise; circulating water heaters require recirculation and separate stored volume and typically have lower input caps (e.g., ≤75,000 Btu/h), limiting their ability to substitute for instantaneous units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE used these design/control distinctions and statutory input caps to argue circulating units are unlikely direct substitutes for instantaneous products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment submission requirements and confidentiality rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To submit comments via Regulations.gov you must provide name/contact information; contact info viewable to DOE staff (and publicly visible only as first/last name, organization); do not submit information you want withheld in the comment body. For CBI, submit two copies via email: a confidential copy and a non-confidential copy with the confidential info deleted; comments via Regulations.gov cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include docket number in submissions. DOE will process submissions before posting; if technical issues occur DOE may contact the submitter using provided contact info. For postal/hand submissions, provide items on CD if feasible. No faxes accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed submission formats and technical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments, data, and other information should be submitted electronically in PDF (preferred), Microsoft Word or Excel, WordPerfect, or text (ASCII) format; documents should be in English, not secured/encrypted, free of defects/viruses, and, if possible, carry the electronic signature of the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid special characters and encryption. DOE may be unable to consider comments it cannot read or clarify if author contact cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign form-letter submission guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit campaign form letters by the originating organization in batches of between 50 to 500 form letters per PDF or as one form letter with a list of supporters' names compiled into one or more PDFs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces comment processing and posting time and helps DOE handle high-volume submissions efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process Rule comment-period deviation justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(f)(2) of the Process Rule specifies a public comment period for a NOPR of not less than 75 calendar days; DOE may deviate for limited-scope SNOPRs and provide a shorter comment period when the agency believes it still provides a meaningful opportunity to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this SNOPR (limited to circulating water heater categorization), DOE provided a shorter comment period (comments due January 10, 2024) and explained the deviation in the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: DOJ Antitrust input per EPCA
rubrics_metrics.description: EPCA requires the Attorney General to provide DOE a written determination whether the proposed standard is likely to lessen competition; DOJ Antitrust Division invites input from market participants on competitive impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested persons may contact energy.standards@usdoj.gov by the date in DATES and should indicate the title and docket number in the subject line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard-setting mandate (maximum technologically feasible & economically justified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 42 U.S.C. 6295(m) and related provisions, DOE must establish amended energy conservation standards designed to achieve the maximum improvement in energy efficiency that DOE has determined to be both technologically feasible and economically justified (6295(o)(2)(A) and 6295(o)(3)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE must identify and consider reasonable regulatory alternatives and select the most cost-effective and least burdensome alternative consistent with law (UMRA section 205); DOE's supporting Technical Support Document (TSD) documents these analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality and peer review requirement for influential scientific information
rubrics_metrics.description: Under OMB's Final Information Quality Bulletin for Peer Review, certain scientific information (including energy conservation standards development analyses) must be peer reviewed by qualified specialists because it is 'influential scientific information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE conducted formal peer reviews of its analytical methodologies and engaged the National Academy of Sciences to review methods for setting building and equipment performance standards; DOE is evaluating the resulting report to improve analyses.
